new_statements.quote: While the normal vowels are used for soft sound, the accented vowels are used for stressed sound. [Rule 1:] Whenever hard vowels are required, Rohingyalish uses another set of vowels (á, é, í, ó, ú), which are normally known as accented (gutá) vowels. [...] Bak = tiger / Bák = share; Bet = cane stick / Bét = intention; Kil = punch / Kíl = wedge; Zor = fever / Zór = rain; Ful = hole/bridge / Fúl = flower. [Rule 2:] Rohingyalish has a total of (12) basic vowels where six are of the soft-sounds and the other six are of hard-sounds.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Rohingya has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing to agree or disagree with. This source adds that the Rohingyalish orthography marks a lexical 'stressed/hard' vs 'soft' vowel contrast with an acute accent, contrastive even in monosyllables; it does not supply a word-stress placement rule, so the catalog rule should stay empty (or be marked as an orthographic vowel-register contrast, not positional stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work is an orthography guide, not a phonological description. It says the acute-accented vowels á é í ó ú write a 'stressed' or 'hard' sound and the plain vowels a e i o u a 'soft' (and short) sound, giving twelve fixed vowel sounds, and it shows the contrast with minimal pairs that are monosyllables (Bak 'tiger' vs Bák 'share', Zor 'fever' vs Zór 'rain'). So what it calls stress is a lexical vowel contrast marked on any vowel of any syllable (examples: Sultán, Fonná, Hañdá, Cúndor, Sáda, Kurá, Córom, Goró, Hóro, Thalasabí, and once two accented vowels in one word, Óroói 'grain for mustard oil'), not a statement about which syllable of a word is prominent. It gives no rule for word-stress placement, no claim that stress is absent, and no mention of tone.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated about accent; the only dialect remark is that h-initial vs vowel-initial doublets (áñti / háñti 'elephant', áñc / háñc 'duck') differ between north and south Arakan (Rule 7)
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes 'Rohingyalish', the Rohingya Language Foundation's Latin orthography for Rohingya of Arakan State (Rakhine), Myanmar; no dialect is specified for the vowel system, and the only dialect remark concerns north vs south Arakan h-initial doublets (Rule 7).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all deciding passages (Kuykendall 2025 pp.18, 20, 45) and the supporting Largin & Erden 2019 passage are verbatim in the text files we hold at the stated locations. (2) The deciding source is a 2025 MA thesis on reduplication whose prosodic remarks are avowedly preliminary; but every reachable source agrees that (a) the acute-marked vowel contrast is lexical and occurs in monosyllables (gór/gor, fúl/ful, bái/bai, kíl/kil, zór/zor), (b) long vowels carry rising (aá) vs falling (áa) contrasts, encoded as three tone signs in the Hanifi script (held Unicode proposals), and (c) no positional word-stress rule is stated anywhere; IOM 2022 (downloaded now, p.15) calls the stress/tone system an open question. That supports classification tonal with qv tonal-OR-pitch accent and an empty positional rule.
